paper.author: D. H. Bailey
paper.title: A Compendium of BBP-Type Formulas for Mathematical Constants

notation.P: P(s, b, n, A) = sum_{k>=0} b^(-k) sum_{j=1..n} a_j/(kn+j)^s
notation.expressions: ASCII; ^ is exponentiation; functions log, sqrt, atan, acos, zeta, cl(n, t) (Clausen: sum cos(kt)/k^n for odd n, sum sin(kt)/k^n for even n); constants pi, phi = (1+sqrt 5)/2, catalan; I is the imaginary unit, clog the complex logarithm, re the real part
notation.formula content: type P: lhs = sum of coef * P(s, b, n, A); type series: lhs = constant_term + prefactor * sum_{k>=k0} term; zero relations are type P with lhs 0
notation.reading: 'read from text' = text layer of the PDF (superscripts recovered from glyph positions); 'read from page image' = read on the rendered page; 'uncertain reading' = marked as such
notation.ids: the paper's equation number; pNN.x = unnumbered item on page NN; 9.pN, 14.a/b, 15.a/b, 16.a/b = list entries; T1.rNN = row of Table 1 (left column first); 80a = the unnumbered formula between (79) and (80); 109+ and 109- = the two signs of (109)

content.statement: Formula (1) lets one compute the n-th hexadecimal or binary digit of pi without the earlier digits, by an algorithm that needs no multiple-precision arithmetic (cited to [14]).
Formula (1) was found by S. Plouffe with an integer-relation program.
According to Craig-Wood [22] (2023), Euler published formulas (2) and (3) in 1779; that they have the digit-extraction property was recognized only in 1997.

entries.reading_note: printed as (1/2^26) sum over k >= 0 of (-1)^k 2^(-30k) times 21 fractions c/(60k+j); the 21 numerators and offsets read on the page image and from the text layer (they agree)

content.statement: Formula (2) had been found by Adamchik and Wagon [1]; formula (3) is in Arndt-Haenel [13, p. 227], ascribed to Pschill.
Borwein, Galway and Borwein [18] (2004) showed that there is no degree-1 BBP-type formula for pi other than those whose base is a power of two.
pi^2 has both a base-2 formula (formula 29) and a base-3 formula (formula 76).
log 2 also has the digit-extraction property, through formula (4) (cited to [14]).
Any constant C = sum over k >= 0 of p(k)/(q(k) b^k), with p, q integer polynomials, deg p < deg q and q without zeros at the non-negative integers, has the digit-extraction property in base b.

entries.reading_note: unnumbered; the four fractions of formula (1) combined into one

content.statement: Hypothesis A (from [16]): for r_n = p(n)/q(n) with integer polynomials, 0 <= deg p < deg q, no poles at positive integers, and an integer b >= 2, the sequence x_0 = 0, x_n = (b x_(n-1) + r_n) mod 1 either has a finite attractor or is equidistributed in [0, 1).
Under Hypothesis A every BBP-type constant is either normal to base b or rational (shown in [16]); no proof of Hypothesis A is known.
If the iteration x_n = frac(2 x_(n-1) + 1/n), x_0 = 0, is equidistributed in [0, 1), then log 2 is normal to base 2.
If the iteration x_n = frac(16 x_(n-1) + (120 n^2 - 89 n + 16)/(512 n^4 - 1024 n^3 + 712 n^2 - 206 n + 21)), x_0 = 0, is equidistributed in [0, 1), then pi is normal to base 16 and to base 2.

Lagarias [26] relates BBP-type constants to G-functions and to a conjecture of Furstenberg, which suggests a special role for constants with BBP-type formulas in two or more bases (for example 2 and 3).

Method: to look for alpha = (1/r) sum_k b^(-k) sum_j a_j/(kn+j)^s, compute alpha and the n sums sum_k 1/(b^k (kn+j)^s) to high precision and run PSLQ on the (n+1)-vector; a relation (a_0, ..., a_n) gives alpha = -(1/a_0) sum_k b^(-k) sum_j a_j/(kn+j)^s.

entries.reading_note: unnumbered example of a telescoping sum

content.statement: A formula with base b and length n can be rewritten as a formula with base b^r and length rn.
A rational combination of two BBP series with the same base is one BBP series; if the bases are b^r and b^s, the sum is one series of base b^lcm(r,s) (cited to [16]).
Many listed formulas have variants obtained by adding a rational multiple of a zero relation; the text says these relations are listed in Section 11.
Definition: P(s, b, n, A) = sum over k >= 0 of b^(-k) sum over j = 1..n of a_j/(kn+j)^s, with s, b, n integers and A = (a_1, ..., a_n) a vector of integers.
The P-notation formulas of the paper were checked by a program that parses the LaTeX source and evaluates both sides to 2000 decimal digits.
log n has a binary BBP formula whenever every prime factor p of n has one for log p (combine the series).

entries.reading_note: the chain of equalities printed before formula (8)

content.statement: By looking at the factorizations of 2^n + 1 and 2^n - 1 one finds many more primes p for which log p has a binary BBP formula.

entries.reading_note: unnumbered; attributed to R. Harley [24]

content.statement: The Taylor series of Re log(1 +- (1+i)/2^n) is a binary BBP-type formula (Harley), which extends the list of primes.

entries.reading_note: unnumbered

content.statement: Both families of results (factors of 2^n +- 1 and Harley's) come from the single expression Re log(1 +- (1+i)^k/2^n) (J. Borwein).

content.statement: List (9) of 46 primes: a preliminary list was given in [14] and has been extended by the author.
List (9) is certainly not complete.
It is unknown whether log p has a binary BBP formula for every prime p.
It is unknown whether the set of primes p for which log p has a binary BBP formula is finite or infinite.
The formulas for log p, for the primes of list (9), are straightforward to derive (not shown in the paper).
Logarithms of certain integers and rationals also have BBP formulas in non-binary bases; formula 84 (base ten) was used in [14] to compute the ten-billionth decimal digit of log(9/10).
Formula (10) was observed by Adamchik and Wagon [1].
The rationals q for which the author found binary BBP formulas for arctan q by PSLQ coincide, in the cases studied, with the q = |Im T/Re T| or |Re T/Im T| of the products T of (11).
Definition: T = product over k = 1..m of (1 +- (1+i)^(u_k)/2^(v_k))^(w_k).
For such q, arctan q has a binary BBP formula, because Im log T is a linear combination of terms whose Taylor series are binary BBP formulas (observation of J. Borwein; see also [17, p. 344]).
Alternative form: T = product over k = 1..m of (1 +- i/2^(t_k))^(u_k) (1 +- (1+i)/2^(v_k))^(w_k), with non-negative integer vectors t, u, v, w.

content.statement: Formulas 90 and 91 appeared in [16]; 92-110 are due to Adegoke [7]; formula 103 was first obtained by Oliver Lafont [31].

The zero relations listed were found with the author's PSLQ program and most are new; not all known ones are listed (the author has a complete set); rewritings to base b^r, length rn are not listed; Table 1 gives the total number of linearly independent zero relations for each (s, b, n), rewritings and unlisted relations included.

In an integer-relation search for a formula, known zero relations must be excluded, for instance by replacing the input entry at the position of each relation's last non-zero coefficient by an unrelated number.
There are five zero relations with s = 1, b = 2^12, n = 24; they are given as formulas 113 through 118.
In relations 113 through 118 the last non-zero entries are at positions 23, 22, 21, 20 and 19 respectively (so entries 19 to 23 of the PSLQ input are replaced by e, e^2, ..., e^5).
As far as anyone can tell (not proven), e is not a polylogarithmic constant in the sense of the paper, and e and its powers are not expected to satisfy BBP-type linear relations.
Adding a rational multiple of a zero relation to a formula with the same s, b, n gives a valid variant; infinitely many variants arise so.
Apart from the discussion in [21], it is not understood why zero relations occur for some s, b, n and not for others.
In most but not all cases where a zero relation was found, non-trivial BBP-type formulas with the same parameters were found too; this suggests that results remain to be discovered.
All listed zero relations except the last two are binary.

content.statement: Relation 111 appeared in [14]; 112 and 113 in [16]; 114 and 122 are due to Oliver Lafont [29], who then proved 113-121 [30]; 115-121, 123-126, 130, 131 were found by the author with PSLQ and are now proven; 127-129 are due to Adegoke [4], who also proved 130 and 131 [5].
Relation 126 was proved by Adegoke as the difference of formulas 40 and 48.
Two further formulas are not BBP-type formulas in the strict sense; the first uses the irrational base b = 2/phi = 2 phi - 2, phi the golden mean (the text refers to Section 9 for phi).

content.statement: The D_k form a Lucas sequence, so a variant of the BBP algorithm may exist for (133); formulas 132 and 133 appeared in [16].
Reference [18]: J. M. Borwein, W. F. Galway and D. Borwein, 'Finding and Excluding b-ary Machin-Type BBP Formulae', Canadian Journal of Mathematics 56 (2004), pages given as 1339-1342.
